question.problem: A laboratory test for a particular disease is conducted on some patients. Of the tested patients, $90%$ of those infected and $9%$ of those not infected tested positive for the disease. Only $14%$ of the entire population is infected with the disease. What is the probability that a randomly chosen patient that tested negative is not infected?  Round your answer to four decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Let $D$ be the event that a randomly chosen patient is infected with the disease, and let $T$ be the event they tested positive. Then, we require $P({D}^{′}|{T}^{′}),$ which we can compute using Bayes' theorem.

$$
P({D}^{′}|{T}^{′})=\frac{P({T}^{′}|{D}^{′})P({D}^{′})}{P({T}^{′})}=\frac{P({T}^{′}|{D}^{′})P({D}^{′})}{P({T}^{′}|D)P(D)+P({T}^{′}|{D}^{′})P({D}^{′})}
$$

From the problem statement, we have the following:

- Since the probability of an infected person testing positive is $90%,$ and the probability of a non-infected person testing positive is $9%,$ we have

$$
P({T}^{′}|D)=1-0.9=0.1,\,P({T}^{′}|{D}^{′})=1-0.09=0.91.
$$

- Since only $14%$ of the population has the disease, we have

$$
P(D)=0.14\,P({D}^{′})=1-0.14=0.86.
$$

Therefore, using Bayes' theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({D}^{′}|{T}^{′}) & =\frac{P({T}^{′}|{D}^{′})P({D}^{′})}{P({T}^{′}|D)P(D)+P({T}^{′}|{D}^{′})P({D}^{′})} \\  & =\frac{(0.91)(0.86)}{(0.1)(0.14)+(0.91)(0.86)} \\  & ≈0.9824\end{aligned}
$$

rounded four decimal places.
